caption: People see the delivery fee and assume it's all profit. It really isn't — what's your real take-home after costs?

slides.title:
How I spend
my R16 500
p/m income
Living in Makhanda
slides.body:
Male, 26
Single, lives alone
Job: Delivery rider, Mr D and Uber Eats
Net income: R16 500 p/m (this month)

slides.title: Bike instalment
slides.includes: Financed a 125cc after my first bike was stolen
slides.body: Second bike, better alarm, still not fully paid off.

slides.title: Rent
slides.includes: A room close to the CBD so I'm near the busiest orders
slides.body: I could pay less further out, but then I'm not first to the good areas.

slides.title: Fuel
slides.includes: Petrol for eight, sometimes ten hour days on the road
slides.body: The app doesn't pay for the fuel between drop-offs, only the ones with an order attached.

slides.title: Phone data
slides.includes: Three apps running at once, all day, every day
slides.body: This is basically my second-biggest work cost after the bike.

slides.title: Bike insurance & tracking
slides.includes: Theft cover, since it happened once already

slides.title: Everything else
slides.includes: Bike maintenance & tyres, groceries, funeral policy, airtime top-ups for the apps, a stokvel with two other riders
slides.body: The maintenance alone spikes some months and wrecks the whole plan.

slides.title: What's left
slides.body: Out of R16 500, on a decent month. A bad weather week or a stolen bike and this number goes negative fast.

slides.title: I finally know what this job actually costs me
slides.body:
I put three months of statements into Beyond Horizon and saw that the bike, fuel and data together eat almost a third of what I make.

I didn't realise how thin the margin actually was until I saw it.

No bank login needed.
